cjc-1295-with-dac.summary: A long-acting growth hormone-releasing peptide that users stack with ipamorelin, aiming for a leaner, more muscular look, better recovery and skin.

quick.overview:
CJC-1295 with DAC is a long-acting analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). People use it in growth hormone peptide stacks hoping for a leaner, more muscular body, faster recovery and better-looking skin.

It mimics GHRH at the pituitary, and the DAC attachment binds blood proteins so its action lasts longer than the version without DAC. That sustained signal is meant to raise growth hormone output, which drives the body-composition payoff. Forum users debate pairing it with ipamorelin or tesamorelin versus choosing the no-DAC version; no trials have tested it for appearance.
quick.how: Users typically run it as one part of a growth hormone stack, paired with a growth hormone-releasing peptide such as ipamorelin or with tesamorelin. Forum threads mostly compare the DAC version with the shorter-acting no-DAC version. Posters describe changes in body composition, recovery and skin over weeks to months of use.
quick.risks: It is not an approved medicine, and risks in healthy users have not been defined by the sources available. Forum discussions focus on combinations rather than safety data, and products sold online are unregulated.

angle.text: CJC-1295 with DAC is a long-acting GHRH analogue that users stack with ipamorelin for a leaner, more muscular look, better recovery and skin. Sustained GHRH signalling is meant to raise growth hormone output, which feeds body composition. Its effects on appearance have not been tested in trials.

modified-grf-1-29.summary: A short-acting GHRH analogue (CJC-1295 without DAC) paired with GH-releasing peptides in stacks for better recovery, muscle and a leaner look.

quick.overview:
Modified GRF (1-29), also called Mod GRF or CJC-1295 without DAC, is a lab-made fragment of GHRH tweaked to resist breakdown. Users pair it with a growth hormone-releasing peptide to get short pulses of growth hormone, aiming for better sleep and recovery, more muscle and a leaner look.

It stimulates GHRH receptors on pituitary cells, releasing growth hormone in a brief pulse. Hormone studies describe the two peptide types working together to release more growth hormone than either alone. No clinical trial cited has tested it for appearance, and user reports are anecdotal and mixed.
quick.how: Forum users describe it as the GHRH half of a pairing with GHRP-2, GHRP-6 or ipamorelin. Because it is short-acting, it is used to mimic natural pulses of growth hormone, with users reporting sleep, recovery and body-composition changes over weeks.
quick.risks: It is unapproved and listed as prohibited in sport. A Danish forensic analysis of seized powders found products sold as modified GRF (1-29) contained analogues with an extra glycine added, so what is sold online can differ from the label.

angle.text: Mod GRF (CJC-1295 without DAC) is paired with a GH-releasing peptide to give short growth hormone pulses, with users citing better sleep, recovery and a leaner, more muscular look. The pairing's synergy is described in hormone studies; human trials for appearance have not been run.

ghrp-2-pralmorelin.summary: A potent ghrelin-receptor peptide that triggers growth hormone release, used by peptide users for muscle, recovery and sleep; a diagnostic test drug in Japan.

quick.overview:
GHRP-2 is a lab-made peptide that mimics ghrelin to trigger growth hormone release. Peptide users stack it with GHRH analogues hoping for more muscle, faster recovery, better sleep and sometimes height, and prefer it to GHRP-6 because it tends to cause less hunger.

It binds the ghrelin receptor in the pituitary and hypothalamus, driving growth hormone release through a path separate from GHRH. Human trials show it raises growth hormone and it is used in Japan as a diagnostic test for adult growth hormone deficiency. None cited tested muscle or looks in healthy people, and a 2020 review noted clinical efficacy data for growth hormone secretagogues remain limited.
quick.how: In peptide communities it is commonly combined with a GHRH analogue such as sermorelin or modified GRF (1-29). Users run it for muscle, recovery and body-composition goals over weeks to months.
quick.risks: It raises appetite, and animal studies show increased appetite and fat mass. Long-term safety data for cosmetic use are lacking, and it is not approved for body-composition use.

angle.text: GHRP-2 is used to raise growth hormone for more muscle, faster recovery, better sleep and sometimes height. It stimulates the ghrelin receptor to release growth hormone, and users like it for causing less hunger than GHRP-6. It is a diagnostic agent in Japan; trials have measured hormone release rather than appearance.

hexarelin-examorelin.summary: A potent growth hormone-releasing peptide used alone or with a GHRH analogue for muscle gain with less water retention, studied for hormone release since the 1990s.

quick.overview:
Hexarelin is a lab-made peptide that mimics ghrelin to prompt a strong growth hormone release. In peptide circles it is regarded as the most potent of its class and is used for muscle gain and recovery, with users describing less water retention.

It activates the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor, and also CD36 in the heart. Reviews describe it as more stable and more potent than ghrelin itself. Human studies since the mid-1990s in healthy volunteers, people with GH deficiency and elderly adults measured hormone responses; none measured muscle, fat or appearance.
quick.how: Users run it alone or paired with a GHRH analogue, and forum posters favour it as a potent and inexpensive growth hormone peptide. Because the response may fade, some discuss breaks between uses.
quick.risks: In some studies it also raised cortisol and prolactin. A 16-week study in healthy elderly people was designed to test whether the growth hormone response weakens with long use, which investigators called a potentially serious limitation. It is not an approved medicine.

angle.text: Hexarelin is regarded as the most potent growth hormone-releasing peptide, used alone or with a GHRH analogue for muscle gain with less water retention. It was studied in 1990s endocrine trials for hormone release; its appearance effects have not been tested, and a fading response with repeated use is discussed.

bimagrumab.summary: An investigational antibody that blocks muscle's growth brakes; trials show fat loss with lean mass kept or gained, but it is not available outside studies.

quick.overview:
Bimagrumab is an antibody that blocks the activin receptors that restrain muscle growth. Appearance communities follow it as a way to lose fat while keeping or adding muscle, the leaner, more muscular look many people want.

It occupies ActRIIA and ActRIIB, stopping myostatin, activins and GDF11 from signalling, which lets muscle grow and affects fat tissue. A phase 2 trial in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity reported significant fat loss and lean mass gain over 48 weeks. Trials in sarcopenia and inclusion body myositis increased muscle mass, though strength or function gains were not demonstrated. Eli Lilly is now testing it alongside GLP-1 drugs to protect muscle during weight loss.
quick.how: It is investigational only and given by intravenous infusion in clinical trials, so there is no routine way to use it outside studies. Current research pairs it with incretin drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.
quick.risks: It is not approved for any use. Reported side effects include muscle spasms, diarrhoea and acne, according to an AI-generated summary of the trials. Strength or function gains were not demonstrated in older adults.

angle.text: Bimagrumab is an investigational antibody that blocks activin receptors, the brakes on muscle growth, and is followed as a route to lose fat while keeping or adding muscle. Trials report fat loss with lean mass gain or preservation in people with obesity; it is not available outside studies.

survodutide.summary: An investigational once-weekly glucagon/GLP-1 injection in phase 3 that cuts appetite and raises energy use, leading to lower body fat; not yet approved.

quick.overview:
Survodutide is a once-weekly injection that activates both glucagon and GLP-1 receptors. People interested in the next generation of weight-loss peptides follow it for the lower body fat and leaner look that fat loss brings.

GLP-1 activation reduces appetite, while glucagon receptor activation is thought to raise energy expenditure and act on the liver. Phase 2 trials reported weight loss and liver benefits, and phase 3 results in obesity and in obesity with fatty liver disease were published in 2026. The trials were in people with obesity, not cosmetic use.
quick.how: Boehringer Ingelheim is developing it for obesity, type 2 diabetes and MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) as a weekly injection. Access is through clinical trials only.
quick.risks: It is not approved, and safety is still under evaluation in phase 3 and cardiovascular outcomes trials. As a GLP-1-class drug, questions include muscle, bone and gastrointestinal effects.

angle.text: Survodutide is a once-weekly glucagon and GLP-1 injection followed by people interested in stronger fat loss. It lowers appetite and is thought to raise energy use, leading to lower body fat and a leaner look. Phase 2 and 3 trials in obesity and fatty liver disease report weight loss; it is not approved.

vk2735.summary: An investigational weekly GLP-1/GIP injection (oral form in trials) in phase 3; phase 2 showed about 9 to 15% weight loss in 13 weeks.

quick.overview:
VK2735 is an investigational dual agonist of the GLP-1 and GIP receptors, aimed at strong fat loss and a leaner look. People seeking large fat loss watch it as a rival to tirzepatide, which acts on the same pair of receptors.

By activating those receptors it reduces appetite and affects metabolism, so body fat falls. In a 13-week phase 2 trial in adults with obesity or overweight, mean weight loss ranged from 9.1% to 14.7% depending on dose, versus 1.7% with placebo. Phase 3 trials began in 2025.
quick.how: Viking Therapeutics is testing it as a weekly injection and as a daily oral tablet. It is available only through clinical trials, and no use outside medical studies for appearance has been documented.
quick.risks: Safety is still being assessed in phase 3. The 13-week phase 2 trial was short, so long-term effects are unknown, and it is not approved as a medicine.

angle.text: VK2735 is an investigational GLP-1/GIP injection watched by people seeking strong fat loss. It shrinks appetite, lowering body fat and giving a leaner look. A 13-week phase 2 trial reported roughly 9 to 15 percent weight loss, and phase 3 is underway.

cagrisema.summary: A not-yet-approved weekly semaglutide plus cagrilintide shot that cut weight about 20% in phase 3 trials, bringing lower body fat.

quick.overview:
CagriSema is a once-weekly injection combining semaglutide with cagrilintide, an amylin analogue. People chasing large fat loss discuss it, sometimes alongside retatrutide, for the lower body fat and leaner look that comes with substantial weight loss.

Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors and cagrilintide activates amylin receptors; both reduce appetite through partly different pathways. A phase 3a trial in adults without diabetes found about 20% mean weight change over 68 weeks versus about 3% with placebo. It beat semaglutide alone in a meta-analysis of early trials, and in a developer-reported head-to-head trial it did not meet non-inferiority against tirzepatide.
quick.how: Novo Nordisk is developing it as a weekly injection for adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes. It is used within clinical trials, and a new drug application was filed with the US FDA in December 2025.
quick.risks: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation are the most reported effects, and were more frequent than with semaglutide alone. It has no approved label, and any supply outside trials is unregulated.

angle.text: CagriSema is a weekly cagrilintide and semaglutide shot used by people after large fat loss, sometimes compared with retatrutide. The two drugs cut appetite through different pathways, lowering body fat. Phase 3 trials showed about 20 percent weight loss in people with obesity; it is not approved.

exenatide.summary: The original GLP-1 injection, approved for type 2 diabetes in 2005, which curbs appetite and brings modest weight loss; later GLP-1 drugs are stronger.

quick.overview:
Exenatide was the first GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for type 2 diabetes. Users mention it as an early route to appetite control and fat loss, though semaglutide and other later drugs now overshadow it.

It mimics GLP-1: it raises insulin release when glucose is high, lowers glucagon, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite. It is a synthetic version of a peptide found in Gila monster saliva. Trials and reviews describe modest weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes, averaging 2 to 3 kg over six months in one cited summary.
quick.how: It is injected under the skin, either twice daily (Byetta) or as a once-weekly extended-release form (Bydureon). In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it appears mostly as an early example of the class, in 2005 to 2009 threads. Using it for fat loss is off-label.
quick.risks: The label warns of pancreatitis, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, kidney injury from dehydration and severe gastrointestinal effects. Nausea is common. It is prescription-only and not licensed for weight loss.

angle.text: Exenatide, the original GLP-1 injection, is mentioned by users as an early route to appetite control and fat loss, now overshadowed by semaglutide. It lowers appetite and slows stomach emptying. Trials in type 2 diabetes show modest weight loss; use for appearance is off-label.

tesofensine.summary: An unapproved oral appetite suppressant that blocks dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake; a 24-week trial found 4.5% to 10.6% extra weight loss over placebo.

quick.overview:
Tesofensine is an oral drug promoted for strong appetite suppression and fat loss, and some users see it as an alternative to approved weight-loss drugs. It was first tested for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, then pursued for obesity after trial participants lost weight.

It blocks the reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, raising their levels in the brain; in animals this reduces appetite through hypothalamic circuits. In a 24-week phase II trial in 203 obese adults published in The Lancet in 2008, placebo-adjusted weight loss ranged from about 4.5% to 10.6% across the three doses tested.
quick.how: It is a daily oral drug. Later work combined it with metoprolol (Tesomet) for rare forms of obesity. On looksmax.org it is discussed as a weight-loss option that users source outside regulated channels.
quick.risks: Reported effects include dry mouth, nausea, insomnia and increases in heart rate and blood pressure. Related drugs such as sibutramine were withdrawn for safety reasons. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA, and supply outside trials is unregulated.

angle.text: Tesofensine is promoted for strong appetite suppression and fat loss. It blocks reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, so you eat less and carry less body fat. A 24-week trial found weight loss beyond placebo of about 4.5 to 10.6 percent, with raised heart rate and blood pressure; it is not approved.

orlistat.summary: A capsule taken with meals that blocks fat absorption, adding a few kilos of weight loss over placebo, with oily stools as the trade-off.

quick.overview:
Orlistat is a capsule that blocks the enzymes that digest dietary fat, so less fat from a meal is absorbed. It is used during cutting phases for gradual fat loss, and some in fat-loss forums described it as a replacement for ephedrine.

It inhibits lipase enzymes in the stomach and pancreas, so part of the fat in a meal leaves in the stool, and very little enters the bloodstream. Trials, including a 1998 European study and a 2-year US trial, found more weight loss than placebo, about 2 to 3 kg extra over 6 to 12 months in one summary. Weight loss is smaller than with newer injectable drugs.
quick.how: It is taken with meals: 60 mg Alli is sold over the counter, 120 mg Xenical by prescription. It is used alongside a reduced-calorie diet. It works less for people already eating low-fat, and some forum posters report diarrhea and little benefit.
quick.risks: Oily spotting, urgency, gas and loose stools are common, reported in more than 25% of patients in one review, especially after fatty meals. It can reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and the label warns against use after organ transplant or with cyclosporine.

angle.text: Orlistat is used during cutting phases to absorb less dietary fat, so fewer calories reach the body and fat comes off gradually. Trials show a few kilos of weight loss over placebo. Oily stools are a known effect, and it works less for people already eating low-fat.

naltrexone-bupropion-contrave.summary: A prescription pill pairing an opioid blocker with an antidepressant to curb appetite and cravings, giving solid but modest weight loss next to GLP-1 drugs.

quick.overview:
Contrave is a daily extended-release tablet combining naltrexone and bupropion, approved for chronic weight management in adults with obesity or overweight. People seeking fat loss without injections follow it for the lower body fat that results from eating less.

Bupropion raises dopamine and noradrenaline and activates appetite-suppressing neurons in the hypothalamus, while naltrexone blocks the opioid feedback that would otherwise damp that effect, so appetite and cravings fall. Phase 3 trials (COR-I, COR-II, COR-BMOD) compared it with placebo over about 56 weeks. Network meta-analyses rank its average weight loss below semaglutide and tirzepatide.
quick.how: It is a prescription pill taken daily alongside diet and exercise. It has also been studied for binge-eating disorder and methamphetamine use disorder. No community discussion specific to the drug appears in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Constipation is reported in about 20% of users of centrally acting weight drugs; nausea, headache and insomnia are also reported. Bupropion carries warnings about suicidal thoughts and seizure risk and can raise blood pressure. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Contrave is a prescription pill used for appetite and craving control, followed by people seeking fat loss without injections. Eating less brings lower body fat and a leaner look. Trials show solid weight loss over placebo, though less than GLP-1 drugs.

phentermine.summary: A decades-old prescription stimulant appetite suppressant used for short-term cutting, with modest weight loss and cardiovascular warnings.

quick.overview:
Phentermine is a prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite and has been used for short-term weight loss since 1959. It is one of the most prescribed obesity drugs in the US and appears in many forum fat-loss stacks, aimed at lower body fat through eating less.

It is an amphetamine-like sympathomimetic amine that releases norepinephrine in the brain, which reduces hunger. Weight loss is modest, about 3.6 kg more than placebo at 12 weeks per one summary, and smaller than with newer incretin drugs. It is also one half of Qsymia (phentermine/topiramate).
quick.how: It is taken as a short-term adjunct, usually described as a few weeks, alongside diet, exercise and behavior change. Brands include Adipex-P, Lomaira and Duromine.
quick.risks: Labels warn of rare pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease, and of raised blood pressure, insomnia and dependence-related withdrawal. It is a controlled substance and contraindicated in pregnancy. The 1990s fen-phen combination was linked to heart valve damage, which led to fenfluramine's withdrawal.

angle.text: Phentermine is a decades-old prescription appetite suppressant used for short-term weight loss and cutting. It cuts hunger so you eat less and lose body fat. Trials show modest loss over weeks to months, and it appears in many forum fat-loss stacks.

phentermine-topiramate-qsymia.summary: A once-daily phentermine plus topiramate capsule for chronic weight management, with clear weight loss over placebo, behind GLP-1 injections.

quick.overview:
Qsymia pairs phentermine, a stimulant appetite suppressant, with topiramate, an anticonvulsant, in a single daily capsule. It is discussed as a non-injection route to fat loss, bringing the lower body fat that comes from eating less.

Phentermine raises norepinephrine release to reduce hunger, while topiramate is thought to add satiety through other brain pathways, so together they lower appetite more than either alone. Phase 3 trials (CONQUER, SEQUEL, EQUIP) show more weight loss than placebo, and network meta-analyses place incretin injections ahead of it. It was approved in 2012 and extended to adolescents in 2022.
quick.how: It is a once-daily extended-release capsule used for chronic weight management. It has also been studied in binge-eating disorder and bulimia, in adolescents and after bariatric surgery.
quick.risks: Reported effects include tingling, dry mouth, constipation, insomnia, cognitive slowing and increased heart rate. Topiramate in pregnancy is associated with oral clefts and birth defects. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Qsymia is a once-daily capsule for chronic weight management and discussed as a non-injection route to fat loss. It lowers appetite and boosts fullness, so you eat less and carry less body fat. Trials show clear weight loss over placebo, though less than GLP-1 injections.

clenbuterol.summary: An asthma-drug stimulant used as a gray-market cutting pill for a leaner, more defined look, with a documented record of heart problems.

quick.overview:
Clenbuterol is a beta-2 agonist made as an asthma bronchodilator. Bodybuilders and others buy it online as a cutting pill for a shredded, more vascular look, sometimes stacked with DNP, and users compare it with GLP-1 drugs as a cheap fat-loss pill.

It activates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, which relax airways and, in muscle and fat tissue, are linked to protein accretion and fat breakdown. A 1995 review described athletes' use for purported anabolic effects and fat reduction, and rodent studies reported body-composition effects. A 2025 randomized trial in 11 healthy men found increased lean mass and muscle protein accretion alongside reduced cardiorespiratory fitness.
quick.how: It is bought through gray-market channels as a pill for cutting phases and often combined with other compounds. Receptors can become less responsive with repeated use, so users discuss on-and-off patterns.
quick.risks: Case reports in athletes describe tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, chest pain, myocarditis, heart attack and death. It is not approved for human use in the US, is banned in sport and in food animals, and unregulated supply can be mislabeled or contaminated.

angle.text: Clenbuterol is a gray-market cutting pill said to give a shredded, more vascular look. It stimulates beta-2 receptors, raising metabolic rate and fat breakdown. It was developed as an asthma drug, and a 2025 trial in 11 healthy men found added lean mass alongside lower cardiorespiratory fitness.

2-4-dinitrophenol-dnp.summary: A 1930s diet drug that turns cells into heaters for very fast fat loss; it is banned for human use because the gap between effective and dangerous doses is narrow.

quick.overview:
DNP is an industrial chemical that was sold as a diet pill in the 1930s. It resurfaced in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles as a very fast fat burner, with users reporting around 8 to 10 lb of fat loss in three weeks and comparing it with GLP-1 options.

It acts as a mitochondrial uncoupler, shuttling protons across the membrane so cells burn fuel and release the energy as heat instead of making ATP. Metabolic rate rises, and so does body temperature. The fat-loss effect is documented from historical case experience and forum reports; no modern controlled trials exist.
quick.how: Users describe cutting cycles lasting a couple of weeks to a few weeks, often alongside other compounds. It is sold online as an industrial or research chemical, not as a medicine.
quick.risks: Reported harms include overheating (hyperthermia) up to fatal temperatures, cataracts, rash, and blood and organ damage. Regulators and toxicology literature describe a very narrow gap between effective and dangerous doses, and there is no antidote. It is not approved for human use; the UK made it a regulated poison in 2023, a seller has been convicted of manslaughter, and WADA bans it.

angle.text: DNP is used by some bodybuilders as a fast cutting drug, with users reporting around 8 to 10 lb of fat loss in three weeks. It uncouples cellular energy production so the body burns fuel as heat, raising metabolic rate. It was sold as a diet drug in the 1930s, and its safety margin is very narrow.

ephedrine.summary: The stimulant in the classic ECA stack, used for appetite suppression and energy while cutting; it raises pulse and pressure, and the FDA banned it from supplements.

quick.overview:
Ephedrine is a stimulant from Ephedra plants, used medically to raise blood pressure during anesthesia. In looksmaxxing it is known as the ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin (ECA) stack, used for appetite suppression and energy during fasted cardio while cutting toward a leaner physique.

It stimulates adrenergic receptors and triggers norepinephrine release, which raises heart rate, blood pressure, alertness and energy expenditure and suppresses appetite. A 2003 JAMA meta-analysis examined it for weight loss and athletic performance, and a general reference summarises the findings as modest short-term weight loss, about 0.9 kg per month more than placebo. It is a milder thermogenic than clenbuterol or DNP.
quick.how: Guides on looksmax.org describe it as increasing energy and reducing hunger during a cut, typically as the ECA stack, with heart-health cautions attached. Forum users also pair it with MK-677 to offset hunger.
quick.risks: Reported effects include palpitations, fast heart rate, high blood pressure, restlessness and nausea, with more heart-related events than placebo in the meta-analysis. The FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid dietary supplements in 2004; the injectable is prescription-only.

angle.text: Ephedrine is the stimulant in the classic ECA stack, used to suppress appetite and lift energy for fasted cardio while cutting toward a leaner physique. It works by stimulating adrenergic receptors and releasing norepinephrine. Trials show modest fat loss, with raised heart rate and blood pressure.

sibutramine.summary: A withdrawn prescription appetite suppressant that helped people lose a few extra kilograms but raised cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients.

quick.overview:
Sibutramine was a prescription weight-loss pill that made people feel full sooner. Cutting forum users saw it as a substitute for or complement to an ECA stack, aimed at lower body fat through eating less.

It blocks reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine in the brain, increasing fullness and reducing food intake. Randomised trials found it produced modest weight loss beyond diet and exercise. In 2010 the SCOUT outcomes trial in more than 10,000 overweight or obese people with cardiovascular disease or diabetes found more heart attacks and strokes, and regulators suspended or withdrew it.
quick.how: It was sold as Meridia (US) and Reductil (elsewhere) and has only scattered mentions on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, where users compared it with ECA stacks before and after withdrawal. It is also known as an undeclared ingredient in some weight-loss supplements.
quick.risks: Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, dry mouth, insomnia and constipation, and a case report of psychosis. Regulators withdrew it in the EU and US in 2010 over cardiovascular risk.

angle.text: Sibutramine is a withdrawn appetite suppressant that cutting forum users saw as a substitute or complement to an ECA stack. It blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake so you feel full sooner and eat less. Randomised trials found modest weight loss beyond diet and exercise.

ketoconazole.summary: An antifungal dandruff shampoo that hair-loss communities add to finasteride and minoxidil for a calmer scalp, less shedding and thicker hair.

quick.overview:
Ketoconazole is an antifungal. As a 2% shampoo (such as Nizoral) it treats dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, and many hair-loss forum members add it to finasteride and minoxidil routines for a calmer, cleaner scalp, less shedding and thicker-looking hair.

It blocks fungal cell-membrane synthesis, reducing Malassezia yeast and scalp inflammation. Proposed antiandrogen effects on the scalp are discussed but not established. A 2020 systematic review of topical ketoconazole in androgenetic alopecia, covering five small human studies (318 participants), found increased hair shaft thickness and called it a promising adjunctive treatment. Large trials against standard treatments have not been done.
quick.how: Users lather the shampoo into the scalp a couple of times a week, as an add-on to finasteride and minoxidil rather than a replacement. The US label lists dandruff and tinea versicolor, not hair loss.
quick.risks: The shampoo can cause mild irritation, dryness or itching in a small share of users, and the label says it is not detected in plasma after chronic scalp use. Oral ketoconazole, a different form, carries an FDA boxed warning for liver injury and drug interactions and is not the form used for hair.

angle.text: Ketoconazole shampoo (Nizoral) is added to finasteride and minoxidil routines for a calmer scalp, less shedding and thicker-looking hair. It reduces scalp yeast and inflammation, and may lower local androgen activity. A 2020 review of five small studies called it a promising adjunct for pattern hair loss.

baricitinib.summary: A prescription JAK-inhibitor pill approved for severe alopecia areata that regrows patchy or total hair loss; not approved for ordinary pattern baldness.

quick.overview:
Baricitinib is a once-daily pill approved for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition causing patchy or total hair loss. Hair communities follow it for its regrowth results, and in June 2022 the FDA approved it as the first systemic treatment for severe alopecia areata in adults.

It blocks JAK1 and JAK2 enzymes, which relay inflammatory cytokine signals, calming the immune attack on follicles so they can resume growth. In the BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 phase 3 trials, more people regrew hair than on placebo at the higher dose. It has not been tested or approved for common male pattern baldness.
quick.how: It is a prescription pill taken daily under medical supervision, with regular monitoring of blood counts, lipids and liver tests. Regrowth is assessed over months of treatment.
quick.risks: The label carries a boxed warning for serious infections, mortality, cancer, major cardiovascular events and blood clots. It is a prescription medicine, and the trial evidence applies to alopecia areata only.

angle.text: Baricitinib is a prescription JAK inhibitor approved for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition causing patchy or total hair loss. It calms the immune attack so follicles resume growth and patches fill in. Two phase 3 trials showed regrowth over placebo; it is not approved for ordinary male pattern baldness.
